title: Family Shari Keller Why Solving Your Child's Summer Boredom Is the Fastest Way to Stop Them from
author: Keller, Shari
summary: Keller argues that modern parents' instinct to rescue children from summer boredom -- with screens, structured activities, and entertainment -- is inadvertently outsourcing their children's internal lives and preventing the development of independent thinking, self-regulation, and genuine curiosity. The piece opens with the image of college students marching into traffic while staring at their phones, and traces this passivity back to a childhood of never having to navigate an empty afternoon without adult-curated input. Keller's central claim is that boredom, when endured rather than escaped, is the condition in which internal architecture is built: children who face the quiet develop the capacity to entertain themselves, imagine, create, and tolerate uncertainty. Drawing on Lenore Skenazy's free-range kids movement and her own childhood experience, Keller argues that even over-scheduled 'educational' alternatives to screen time remain adult-curated experiences that fail to develop genuine independence. The article concludes that stopping the rescue -- letting children get genuinely bored without running interference -- is one of the most countercultural and important things parents can do for long-term development.
points: * The pattern of rescuing children from boredom with screens or scheduled activities outsources their internal lives: children who never navigate an empty afternoon without adult input never develop the internal architecture for self-regulation, independent thought, or genuine curiosity. * Boredom is not an emergency to be extinguished but a condition in which internal development occurs: when children face the quiet without rescue, the brain adjusts and children learn to create, imagine, explore, and tolerate uncertainty. * Even 'educational' alternatives to screen time (museum trips, enrichment camps) can fail if the underlying assumption is that a child's time must always be curated by an adult; the problem is not what replaces the screen but whether the child is ever left to their own devices. * The children walking into traffic while staring at phones are the end product of a childhood in which constant stimulation was treated like oxygen: trained to treat constant input as baseline, with silence as something to eliminate. * Parents who stop rescuing their children from boredom are doing something radically countercultural: trusting the child to develop internal resources that no amount of curated activity can substitute for.
quotes: We have raised a generation of kids who treat constant stimulation like oxygen. The moment the inputs stop -- the second the routine drops away and the silence sets in -- panic happens.

If you want a child who can think for themselves, entertain themselves, and navigate the real world with actual independence, you have to stop rescuing them from the quiet. You have to let them get bored.

The underlying assumption is that a child's time must always be curated by an adult. If it isn't an algorithm providing the entertainment, it must be a parent acting as a cruise director, ensuring that every hour is structured, productive, and educational.

When a child never has to navigate an empty afternoon without a screen or a spreadsheet telling them what to do, they never develop the internal architecture required to self-regulate. They become passive consumers of reality, waiting for the next thing to tell them how to feel and what to think.

I tried to read an entire set of encyclopedias, made it through the letter A, got bored again, and abandoned it for something else. I drew pictures, learned to sew, built stuff, walked around the neighborhood, and just thought about things.
What we are actually doing is outsourcing our children's internal lives.
